BP p.l.c. (BP-GB): investment memo

BP: the balance-sheet repair is finished, the commodity windfall is fading, and the share price offers the dividend and little more

Written 9 November 2026. Share price 624.3p on 29 October 2026 (52-week high 638.5p). All money is in US dollars unless stated. Definitions, sources and the two earnings-per-share series used in this memo are explained in the end notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The bottom line for Richard

BP's risk/reward over the next 12-24 months is not unusually skewed to the positive. At the guideline fair multiple of 12.82x, BP's shares return about -1% to December 2027 and +7% to mid-2029, all of it from dividends. At my own fair multiple of about 12x, the 18-month return is about -7%. The probability-weighted return is close to zero, and the downside would arrive faster than the upside.

The version of BP worth owning is likely to be on offer later and at a lower price: a repaired company running a buyback through a normal oil price, priced on normalised earnings, possibly in late 2027. The two events to watch before then are the buyback framework on 15 December 2026 and the Q4 2026 results in February 2027.

BP is two investment cases in one stock, and over the next 18 months the two cases point in opposite directions.

The first case, a commodity windfall, is at its peak. BP's refining indicator margin (RIM) reached $46.70 a barrel in Q3 2026 against a planning baseline of $10.80, Brent is near $97, and BP's earnings are the most geared to refining margins among European majors. Together these lift FY2026 EPS to about $1.45, from $0.48 in FY2025. Every forecast path normalises the windfall: the model has EPS of $0.86 in FY2027 and $0.64 in FY2028, and the forward curve, consensus and every broker agree on that shape.

The second case, a corporate repair, has moved faster than anyone expected, BP included. Net debt fell from $22.2bn to $13.9bn in nine months and should be about $6bn at end-2026, five quarters ahead of target. The Castrol sale has closed, BP's stock of hybrid bonds is shrinking on a published schedule, the first chief executive recruited from outside BP is running the company with an activist shareholder behind her, and the first buyback framework in two years is due on 15 December. At a similar oil price, the repair lifts normalised EPS 25-40% above the FY2024-25 level, through lower finance costs, hybrid coupons, tax, depreciation and share count, and it keeps the dividend covered down to about $53-56 Brent.

The problem for the next 12-24 months is that BP's share price follows the windfall, not the repair. BP has a beta of 1.18 to a sector that trades near the top of its ten-year multiple range, while the sell-side already knows about the repair and the share price mostly reflects it.

Ten insights that should shape Richard's reading of the case.

  1. FY2026 is a peak in prices and margins, not an operating step change. Refining and trading made up about 28% of BP's FY2026 EBITDA, against a historical share of 9% (Jefferies). Three prices (the refining margin, Brent and trading conditions) explain the whole fall in EBITDA from $56bn in FY2026 to $36bn in FY2028; disposals and cost changes net to almost nothing.
  2. The refining margin, not Brent, is the biggest swing factor in BP's earnings. Each $1 a barrel of RIM is worth $450m of pre-tax profit, so the $35 gap between the 2026 RIM and a normal year is worth more than a $40 move in Brent. Refining margins can unwind within weeks once the physical supply disruption ends.
  3. The balance-sheet repair is the best-evidenced part of the case, and it is finished. BP has hit every balance-sheet target early for six years. The remaining risk lies in how BP uses its new balance-sheet capacity, not in whether that capacity exists.
  4. Normalised EPS will sit above the pre-windfall base, for reasons the market has not fully priced. FY2028-30 EPS of $0.63-0.67 compares with $0.48-0.54 in FY2024-25 at a similar oil price. The uplift comes from below EBIT: finance cost about $1.4bn lower, hybrid coupons $0.25bn lower, a tax rate 3 points lower, depreciation about $1.7bn lower, and buybacks. About 40% of the uplift in net income is lower depreciation, which is real for EPS but adds nothing to cash.
  5. BP's cost savings are real, but most of them leak away before they reach profit. Of the $6.5-7.5bn gross cost target, $2.5bn comes from sold businesses that take their revenue with them, and $3.0bn of offsets (inflation, acquired activity and management choices) has absorbed the rest to date. Operating cost excluding disposals and acquisitions was flat year on year in Q3 2026, and the model credits only $0.4-0.9bn a year of net gain.
  6. Disposals reduce balance-sheet risk but dilute the earnings base. Each dollar of disposal proceeds removes about four times its interest saving in EBITDA. Castrol, BP's steadiest earner, has gone, so the earnings that remain are more cyclical, not less.
  7. The buyback framework due on 15 December is the most important company-specific input for 2027-30. Our base case of $4.5bn of buybacks in 2027 sits above the most constructive broker forecast ($1.5bn) and below what a framework modelled on Shell's would pay ($9-12bn). Each $1bn of buybacks retires about 0.8% of BP's shares.
  8. The sell-side has caught up with the good news. FY2027 consensus EPS is up 35% in three months and 53% in twelve, and 54% of analysts now rate BP a buy. The model's FY2027-28 EPS is at or slightly below where consensus is settling. Favourable surprises are now confined to the balance sheet, the tax rate and the buyback framework, and to the next two events.
  9. BP can now survive the downside, which it could not a year ago. Even at $60 Brent and a $9 RIM, free cash flow covers the dividend and net debt stays below $10bn. A downturn would now land on EPS and the valuation multiple, not on the dividend or the credit rating.
  10. BP's shares are priced near the top of both the sector's valuation range and their own. The two-year-forward P/E was 10.8x on 6 November (ten-year median 9.5x; 75th percentile 12.1x). The guideline fair multiple of 12.82x, applied to a two-year-forward EPS that falls 13% as the forecast window rolls onto FY2029, gives a total shareholder return of -1% to December 2027 and +7% to mid-2029. That return is the central message of this memo.

Implication: BP's per-share mechanics are skewed positive and predictable, its operating earnings are skewed negative and fast-moving, and the share price follows the operating earnings. The attractive version of BP, a repaired balance sheet running a buyback through a normal oil price, is likely to be on offer later and at a lower price. The bull case is real: the forward curve keeps the refining margin at $28 a barrel through 2027, and if the curve is right FY2027 EPS is nearer $1.20 than $0.86. The bull case needs the geopolitical disruption to outlast the restocking of global inventories, however, and it would reveal itself quarter by quarter, whereas the bear case would reveal itself in days.

The five judgements that move the value of BP's shares most, with the arithmetic

All five judgements use one conversion. After tax at 36-37%, and on about 15.3bn shares in FY2027 or 14.5bn in FY2028, $1bn of pre-tax profit is worth about $0.042-0.044 of EPS, $10 a barrel of Brent about $0.14, and $5 a barrel of RIM about $0.10.

Judgement 1: how fast oil prices and refining margins normalise in 2027 (the 18-month driver). The base case assumes Brent at $80, a RIM of $17 and trading profit $0.8bn above normal, which gives FY2027 EPS of $0.86. I put 30% on the bear path, 45% on the base and 25% on the bull path, so the outcomes are balanced in probability but skewed down in speed.

Judgement 2: where the "normal" oil price and refining margin sit for 2028-30 (the value driver). The base case assumes Brent at $70-72 and a RIM of $11-12, which gives model FY2029 EPS of $0.62. This judgement moves the value of the shares more than any other, and it is the one on which the market agrees least: broker FY2028 EPS forecasts range from $0.21 to $0.93.

  • If normal is Brent $65 and a RIM of $10: Brent $5-7 lower costs $1.7-2.4bn and the RIM $1-2 lower costs $0.45-0.9bn, about $3bn pre-tax in all (8% of plateau EBITDA), $1.9bn after tax and $0.13 a share on 14.5bn shares. FY2029 EPS falls to about $0.49 (-21%). At the guideline multiple of 12.82x, that is about $1.65 a share of value, roughly 125p.
  • If normal is Brent $80 and a RIM of $14 (closer to the 2028 forward curve): pre-tax profit rises about $4.8bn, after-tax profit $3.0bn and EPS $0.21. FY2029 EPS rises to about $0.83 (+34%), worth roughly 200p a share at the guideline multiple.
  • Rule of thumb: each $5 of normal Brent is worth about $0.075 of plateau EPS (about 12% of it) and about 70p of value at 12.82x.

Judgement 3: the size of the buyback framework announced on 15 December. The base case assumes buybacks of $4.5bn in 2027, $5.5bn in 2028 and $4.5bn a year after that. On the model's assumed buyback price, those buybacks cut the average share count about 10% by 2030 (about 16% at the lower price in the Analyst's cross-check). Each $1bn retires about 120m shares at today's price, about 0.8% of the count and of EPS.

  • Morgan Stanley's $0.75bn a quarter from Q3 2027 (about $1.5bn in 2027): $3bn less than the base case, about 360m fewer shares retired, and FY2028 EPS about $0.015 lower (-2%).
  • A Shell-type framework paying out 40-50% of operating cash flow (about $9-12bn in 2027, then $8-10bn a year): about $5-7bn a year more than the base case and about $20bn more by end-2030, retiring about 2.4bn more shares (about 17% of the count). FY2030 EPS would be about $0.74 against $0.63 (+17%).
  • The framework matters more for the multiple than for EPS in the next 18 months. Inside 18 months the EPS effect is 1-3%; over three years it is 10-17%. BP's 2027 total cash yield is 5.9% against Shell's 10.1% (Morgan Stanley), and closing half of that gap is plausibly worth one to two multiple points, or 10-15% of the share price.

Judgement 4: what trading and refining capture earn in a calm market (the earnings-quality driver). The base case assumes trading profit at normal from 2028 and refining capture of 50% of a $12 RIM. BP discloses neither its trading profit nor its capture rate, so investors cannot track this judgement; it will show up only as beats and misses against consensus.

  • Downside, a repeat of 2023-24 (six to eight quarters below consensus): trading profit $1.0bn below normal, and capture of 45% instead of 50%, which on a $12 RIM across about 470m barrels of throughput costs about $0.3bn. The total is about $1.3bn pre-tax, $0.8bn after tax and $0.055 a share, taking FY2028 EPS to about $0.585 (-9%).
  • Upside, volatility persists and trading earns its 2020-25 average uplift: about $1bn more pre-tax profit, or $0.04 a share.

Judgement 5: whether absolute operating cost reaches BP's target of about $18bn in 2027 (the self-help driver). The base case assumes $19.0bn in 2027 and $18.3bn in 2028, which credits $0.4bn and $0.8bn of net efficiency against FY2025.

  • If BP delivers $18.0bn in 2027, excluding disposals and acquisitions: pre-tax profit rises $1.0bn, after-tax profit $0.64bn and EPS $0.042 (FY2027 EPS +5%; FY2028 EPS a further $0.03 above base).
  • If oilfield service-cost inflation runs at 4% rather than 2.5% on a $19bn cost base: profit falls about $0.3bn a year, compounding to about $0.02 a share by 2028.
  • Below EBIT, two consensus errors offset each other. Consensus FY2028 finance cost of $2.1bn ignores a floor in BP's finance cost and is about $0.45bn too low (-$0.02 a share). Consensus tax leakage of about 45%, against our 37%, is too high (+$0.03 a share).

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment; absence of headwinds

Evidence. The external environment in 2026 gave BP its strongest earnings backdrop since 2022, and the drivers are already turning. The disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz took Brent from $81 in Q1 2026 to $104 in Q2 and $97 in Q3, and a shortage of middle distillates (diesel and jet fuel) took BP's RIM from $11.90 in Q2 2025 to $46.70 in Q3 2026. BP captured 64% of indicator margins in H1 2026, against 55% for Shell and 35% for TotalEnergies, because it runs the most complex refining system among European majors and the largest trading book. The capital rotation back toward oil producers has also re-rated European majors to the top of their ten-year multiple ranges. The signs of reversal are visible: front-month Brent fell about 16% in the three trading days to 4 November on hopes of a US-Iran agreement, even though the Strait stayed closed; Singapore refining margins have already fallen from above $30 in April to $9 in October; and the forward curve still prices December 2027 Brent at about $88 and forward refining margins at about three times their historical average for December 2027 and twice for December 2028.

Inference. BP's tailwinds are cyclical, geopolitical and short in visibility, while its headwinds are structural and mild. The headwinds (detailed in the figure below) absorb cost savings, drive BP out of its home basin, raise European refining costs, turn liquefied natural gas (LNG) into a buyer's market from 2027 and, through new refining capacity, supply the standard mechanism that reverses product margins. Demand is not the problem: oil demand grows slowly to about 2030, electric vehicles are being adopted more slowly than expected, and LNG demand grows about 6% a year. The problem is that the price of what BP sells is set by a supply disruption that can reverse in weeks.

So what. The external picture is clearly favourable for the next six months and turns against the case over 12-24 months. Q4 2026 still carries a RIM of $30-35 and Brent near $95, but, as the two sector digests put it, "every path normalises margins from 2027". BP is the European major most exposed to that reversal, because refining and trading produced 28% of its FY2026 EBITDA against a historical 9%, and the sale of its North Sea business does not change its post-tax sensitivity to Brent.

Counter-case. The supply disruption could outlast the restocking of inventories. Planned refinery maintenance of 3.4-6.4m barrels a day falls due by mid-2027, Saudi and Kuwaiti refineries have no restart timetable, European diesel stocks are near five-year lows, Russian diesel exports are down 70%, and governments plan to restock 500m barrels. Bernstein's observation that product margins historically stay elevated for hundreds of days after crude prices peak is well founded. If the forward curve is right, FY2027 EBITDA is about $8bn above our base case.

Market view and mine. Consensus follows the forward curve with a lag of one to two quarters, so it sits above our oil-price and margin assumptions for 2027 (Morgan Stanley assumes Brent at $86 and a BP RIM of $27.7). I agree with the market on the direction of prices and on the structural headwinds. I differ on speed: I deliberately set the refining margin, the most reversible line, below the curve, because BP's shares re-price on the forward curve in days while the physical market normalises over quarters. What would change my view: the Strait remaining impaired past mid-2027 with the 2027 Brent curve holding above $85, or evidence that Gulf refining capacity has been damaged rather than idled.

Conclusion on #1: the tailwinds are unusually strong today and are the least durable force in the case, while the structural headwinds are mild, so the external skew over 12-24 months is negative even though the next six months are favourable.

Score: 27, set by the Rater. The external forces that made FY2026 (Hormuz disruption, a $46.70 RIM against a $10.80 planning base, Brent near $97) are a scarcity windfall that every path normalises from 2027, taking revenue down 24% and EBITDA 36% by FY2028, with mild structural headwinds on top (service inflation, the UK 78% tax rate, EU carbon rules, the 2026-28 LNG wave) and demand itself not the problem; the 0.8th-percentile consensus EPS growth tells the truth here. I agree with the group's 28: a clear net negative over two to three years, below Volati's late-cycle declines but not the structural overcapacity of Maersk, and the next six months' favourable deck does not change the two-to-three-year balance.

#2 Internally-driven corporate change forces; absence of problems

Evidence. BP's internal change programme is among the largest in the European sector, and it is delivering on the lines that management controls. Meg O'Neill, the first chief executive in BP's history recruited from outside the company (23 years at ExxonMobil, four running Woodside), took office on 1 April 2026. In seven months she has:

  • halved the segment structure, to two segments from 1 July (reported externally from 1 January 2027);
  • launched the sale of the entire UK North Sea business (about 110,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day) and of Archaea, and closed the Castrol sale (2 November, $6bn net) and the Gelsenkirchen refinery (31 July);
  • sold 5% of Aker BP ($1.06bn), closed the bp Ventures arm and exited the Bay du Nord project;
  • moved the net debt target forward by a year and then beaten it by five quarters;
  • delivered $4.0bn of structural cost reductions by Q3, against a target raised twice to $6.5-7.5bn;
  • set targets to cut total financial obligations to $33-35bn by end-2026 (from $39-41bn) and hybrid bonds to about $9bn by end-2027 (from $12.1bn).

Elliott, the activist investor, holds about 5%, has obtained most of its agenda and still wants more cash returned. Management incentives are 65% financial, 20% operational and 15% safety.

Inference. The change programme is strong, broad and well resourced in capital and board backing, but it is under-resourced in people and its results so far are financial rather than operational. The people strain shows in a workforce down more than 5%, the loss of senior technical staff, employee engagement of 64%, an interim head of Downstream, five non-executive directors gone in a year and a chair removed for misconduct in May. The programme also runs about eight major items at once, against a sensible guardrail of two. On operations, upstream reliability fell to 92.4% in Q2 before recovering to 95.3% in Q3, Tier 1 and 2 process-safety events rose to 18 in Q2 2026 from 5 a year earlier, the Rotterdam refinery had an unplanned outage in October, and upstream unit cost rose 6% to $6.54 per barrel of oil equivalent. The disposals also sell earnings: about $2.6bn of EBITDA leaves in all, and BP receives no income from its retained 35% of Castrol, because the buyer, Stonepeak, holds a preference and about $0.8bn of future dividends was prepaid in the price.

So what. The internal changes lift normalised EPS by about $0.12 a share before buybacks (through interest, hybrid coupons, tax and depreciation), and they fund the buyback that holds EPS flat at $0.62-0.67 through 2028-30 while net income drifts down 8%. They do not offset the normalisation of prices and margins, and they add no volume: production is guided flat to 2027 and to 2.3-2.5m barrels of oil equivalent a day by 2030, a range that the North Sea sale has already made out of date.

Counter-case. Shell's 2023-26 programme shows what this kind of programme can become: $5.8bn of savings delivered three years early (57% of them not from disposals), nineteen consecutive quarters of buybacks above $3bn, a 19% cut in the share count and a dollar return 30% ahead of peers. If O'Neill's December framework and FY2027 cost line follow Shell's template, the internal changes would be worth more than our model credits; on Shell's ratio of gross to net savings, BP's cost target could be raised by about $1bn gross. Against that, BP's programme leans more heavily on disposals, it restarts distributions at the top of a margin cycle rather than in the middle of one, and its framework will be tested against falling oil prices and margins in its first year.

Market view and mine. The sell-side knows about the deleveraging ("the clearest play on de-gearing", Morgan Stanley) and rewards the gross cost number. It also knows that the cost savings are leaking (Redburn: "not yet flowing through") but gives the leak little weight. I agree that internal change is the strongest positive force in the case; I put less weight than the market on the gross cost figure and more on the earnings sold with the disposals. What would change my view: FY2027 absolute operating cost at or below $18bn after removing the effect of disposals, plus two more quarters of upstream reliability above 95% with process-safety events back toward 2025 levels.

Conclusion on #2: internal change is the strongest positive force in the case and is delivering early on every financial line, but its operating proof (costs reaching profit, reliability, volumes) is still outstanding and its disposals shrink the earnings base it is repairing.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. A full, funded, multi-part reset under the first external CEO with an aligned activist (two segments, Castrol and North Sea sales, Gelsenkirchen shut, $4.0bn of structural cost cuts against a target raised twice, net debt target beaten five quarters early) lifts normalised EPS about $0.12 before buybacks plus a 10% share-count fall; it is repair not growth, its outputs are financial rather than operating (Q2 reliability 92.4%, process-safety events up from 5 to 18, upstream unit cost +6%, ex-perimeter opex flat), and the disposals sell about $2.6bn of EBITDA. That is the 75 level held back by lagging outputs and weighty internal problems, coherent with the group's 70, just below Theon's deliberate pivot and above OEM's acquirer turn.

#3 Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile, management

Value chain and industry structure. BP is a mid-ranked integrated oil major with no market power of its own. It produces about 2.2m barrels of oil equivalent a day, ranks fifth among Western majors, and has a market value of about $130bn against ExxonMobil's $620bn and Shell's $240bn. OPEC+ sets crude prices, the marginal refinery sets product margins, and LNG is moving to a buyer's market. The industry structure is supportive on average (capital discipline everywhere, "value over volume", scarce drilling rigs) and unusually supportive in 2026. That support, however, rests on two sets of actors BP cannot influence, OPEC+ and the parties to the Middle East conflict, and OPEC+ has fought for market share twice in a decade (2014-16 and 2020). Market share is consolidating toward companies with advantaged resources: ExxonMobil in the Permian and Guyana, Shell in LNG and through ARC Resources, and TotalEnergies with unit costs below $5 a barrel and a 12-year reserve life. BP is a seller of assets and a plausible takeover target, not a consolidator.

Business model and competitive advantages. BP's genuine advantages sit in the middle of the value chain, and they amplify swings in oil prices and margins rather than offsetting them. The two main advantages, integrated supply, trading and shipping, and complex refining that captures a high share of indicator margins, both earn most when markets are dislocated and shrink in calm years: 2023-24 produced six to eight quarters below consensus. BP's deepwater technology in the Gulf of America and its positions with host governments are moderate advantages. BP lacks the advantages that compound over time in this industry: low unit cost, scale, volume growth and reserve life. Its largest new resource, the Bumerangue discovery off Brazil with 8 billion barrels in place, is an option for the 2030s and is complicated by a high carbon dioxide content.

Financial profile. BP's financial profile is spectacular at today's prices and middling at a normal oil price. Return on average capital employed (ROACE) was 12-14% in 2024-25, against 14% at TotalEnergies and 14.5% at Equinor. BP targets 16% for 2027 at $70 Brent, and the model says BP will beat that target mainly because impairments and disposals shrink the capital base. BP's normal-year EBIT margins of 7-8% are below peers', although the percentage is a poor guide because about 85% of revenue is downstream sales that pass costs straight through. The earnings base is not clean: reported profit was $55m in FY2025 against underlying profit of $7.49bn, and "one-off" impairments recur ($6bn in 2025, $1bn in Q2 2026 and $4bn in Q3). What has changed is the balance sheet. Gearing fell from 22.6% to 14.8% in one quarter, and net debt will be near $6bn at end-2026, so within 15 months BP will have moved from the most levered European major to among the least levered.

Management. O'Neill's team is a promising enabler of change and an unproven operator. In her first seven months O'Neill has shown decisiveness, candour ("plants did not run as expected") and no attachment to legacy assets, and the chief financial officer, Kate Thomson, has executed the deleveraging and admitted that cost cuts are "not moving fast enough" to the bottom line. Against that stand a half-built senior team, a strained culture, a five-year record of strategic reversals (the 2020 pivot to renewables, its 2025 reversal and the February 2026 buyback suspension), minimal insider ownership (about 0.03% of the shares) and the worst distribution record among European majors over six years. Management's stated ambition, to be "fit to grow" and to "compete in our weight class", is right for the balance sheet but is not yet a growth vision.

So what. BP's structure justifies a below-peer, ex-growth multiple until BP shows either volume growth or a covered, buyback-led payout. The shift in mix away from Castrol and toward refining and trading also makes normal-year EPS less predictable, not more.

Counter-case. A repaired balance sheet, mid-chain advantages and a disciplined operator are exactly the combination on which Shell re-rated from 2023, and BP's refining and trading franchise is the best in Europe when markets are dislocated.

Market view and mine. The market agrees with this ranking: BP has taken part in the sector's re-rating at the bottom of the integrated majors, with the weakest twelve-month share-price return among them (see the peer table in #12), and the market is waiting for the buyback framework to narrow BP's discount. I agree with the market here. What would change my view: a Bumerangue flow test that turns the resource into a development BP can book as reserves, or a management team completed with an external head of Downstream followed by two clean operating years.

Conclusion on #3: BP is a mid-ranked price-taker with real but cyclical mid-chain advantages, a newly average balance sheet, below-average returns and reserve life, and a management team whose financial delivery is proven and whose operating delivery is not; these foundations support a dividend and a modest buyback, not a premium multiple.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. Qualitatively a mid-ranked, sub-scale price-taker (OPEC+ and geopolitics set its prices, the lowest proved reserve life among majors at 7.1 years, unit cost above TotalEnergies, a seller and plausible target rather than a consolidator) whose real mid-chain advantages in trading and complex refining are cyclical and amplify the deck; management is a promising operator on a five-year record of reversals. The figures (ROIC about 0% at the 10th percentile, operating margin 25th) overstate the weakness because of impairments and pass-through revenue, but normal ROACE of 12-14% below peers, recurring 'one-off' impairments and less predictable post-Castrol earnings keep it in the 'mediocre business made safe' band, coherent with groups of 32-38, between Teqnion and Zegona.

#4 Conservative guidance; keeping the sell-side conservative; the record of delivery and upgrades

Evidence. BP does not guide profit. It guides inputs at a conservative planning price, and it guides balance-sheet outcomes that it then beats. BP planned 2026 on $80 Brent against an actual average of $93.5, and it sets its mid-term targets at $70 Brent and a $10.80 RIM, against $97 and $46.70 in Q3 2026. The mid-term target of "ROACE above 16% by 2027 at $70" will be met and probably beaten, but mainly because the capital base is smaller. The one target at risk of a quiet miss is absolute operating cost of about $18bn in 2027: our base case is $19.0bn, and Jefferies has already raised its 2027 forecast of non-shale unit cost to $16 per barrel of oil equivalent. BP's record splits cleanly four ways:

  • Early delivery on balance-sheet actions for six years: net debt fell from $40.4bn in Q3 2020 to $20.9bn by end-2023, ahead of target, and the current $14-18bn target was met five quarters early.
  • Beats in volatile quarters: every quarter of 2026 has beaten consensus.
  • Misses in calm quarters: six to eight consecutive misses in 2023-25, and only 23% of the 2023-25 share plan vested.
  • Quiet loosening of the items that cost money: capital expenditure guidance has drifted up, and the tax-rate guidance has moved in both directions.

Inference. BP's guidance is conservative where it is specific (prices, balance sheet, capital expenditure, tax) and ambitious where it is vague (gross cost savings, a return target on a shrinking capital base, and a 2030 production range that includes a basin BP is selling). BP's habit of planning far below spot prices makes FY2026 consensus a floor and the end-2026 balance-sheet targets a certainty, which is helpful. It also means that BP's "beats" in 2026-27 are beats driven by oil prices and margins, and the market already discounts them: BP's shares fell 5% on the day of its Q2 beat.

So what: the 15 December framework decides this topic, and the evidence points to a framework set to be beaten rather than one that stretches. Four facts support that reading:

  • O'Neill called $40bn of total liabilities "too high for optimal resilience in a low-price environment".
  • BP has named the $5.9bn payable for the Gulf of America oil-spill settlement as the first call on excess cash.
  • Woodside, O'Neill's previous company, set a framework of 20-40% of operating cash flow on 5 November.
  • A board that suspended buybacks in February 2026 will want a framework it can sustain at $60-65 Brent.

I expect a payout of 30-40% of operating cash flow with a guardrail on net debt or total obligations, buybacks from February 2027 at $0.75-1.25bn a quarter, a cost target restated (and possibly raised) on the two-segment basis, and a re-based production range. On FY2027 operating cash flow of $28-30bn, that framework implies buybacks of $3-6.5bn after a $5.4bn dividend, and our base case of $4.5bn sits at the centre of that range.

Counter-case. A new chief executive's first framework is a chance to reset expectations upward, not downward. Morgan Stanley expects net debt near zero by mid-2027, which would give room for a Shell-type payout of 40-50% with a catch-up, and Elliott will push for it. The record of BP's leadership also includes a chief executive who, as finance director, delivered $2.5bn of savings six months early.

Market view and mine. The market knows about the balance-sheet beats and expects a buyback restart; the debate is about size, and the more bullish hopes (up to $3bn a year by late 2027, and higher) have about a 50% chance of being disappointed. I agree that BP's guidance is conservative on the specific items, and I put more weight than the market on O'Neill's own words about resilience. What would change my view: a framework paying out more than 40% of cash flow, or a firm commitment to settle the Gulf of America payable in 2027 so that it stops competing with buybacks.

Conclusion on #4: guidance is conservative where it is specific and the delivery record on balance-sheet lines is excellent, but those beats are now visible to everyone, so the only guidance item that can still surprise is the December framework, and the evidence points to measured rather than generous.

Score: 47, set by the Rater. BP guides inputs and balance-sheet outcomes conservatively and beats them (net debt target met five quarters early, six years of early balance-sheet delivery, tax guide cut, proceeds raised), and its planning deck far below spot is genuinely conservative; but within the last three years it missed consensus for six to eight consecutive quarters (2023-25, 23% plan vesting), suspended the buyback in February 2026, loosened capex guidance and holds a vague 2027 cost target at risk of a quiet miss. The guidance group's 52 is pulled down by the sell-side group's 28 and the recent miss record, placing it just below Yara's no-guidance, price-made beats and above Instalco's missed targets.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out scope, feedback loops

Pricing power: none. BP's realised liquids prices were 80-82% of Brent in Q2-Q3 2026, its realised refining margins ran up to $5 a barrel below the indicator margin in early 2026, and its LNG prices are linked to oil with a nine-month lag. Castrol, the one business with demonstrated power to pass on price increases, has been sold. Price is therefore an external input to BP's earnings, not something BP sets.

Operating leverage: very high, symmetric, and currently pointing down. BP's fixed cost base of about $21bn of underlying operating cost plus $17bn of depreciation sits against revenue set by prices, so swings in EBITDA pass almost one for one into EBIT. BP's published sensitivities ($340m of pre-tax profit per $1 of Brent, $450m per $1 of RIM and $40m per 10 cents of Henry Hub gas) explain about 90% of the variance in pre-tax profit, and they reproduce the FY2026-27 EBITDA fall almost exactly (chart below). Volume leverage is small, with 1% of upstream volume worth about $0.2-0.25bn pre-tax, and slightly negative in the near term: Q4 production is guided at 2,090-2,230 thousand barrels of oil equivalent a day, and refining throughput is down about 200,000 barrels a day for maintenance. In a downturn BP's fixed costs do not flex down, but its capital expenditure does: to $13bn, helped by the short investment cycle of bpx energy, BP's US onshore business.

Financial leverage: reversing from an amplifier of risk into an engine of per-share growth. BP's net finance cost falls from $4.0bn in 2025 to about $2.6bn in 2027, toward a floor of about $1.65bn, because lease interest and the unwinding of discount on provisions do not fall with debt. Hybrid coupons fall about $0.25bn. At today's share price, each $1bn of buybacks adds about 0.8% to EPS, against about 0.3% for $1bn of debt repayment, so a dollar of buyback is worth two to three times a dollar of debt repayment. Once net debt is near $6bn, the rational use of BP's spare cash therefore switches to share repurchases.

Cost-out: real in gross terms, small in net terms. About $4.0-5.0bn of the $6.5-7.5bn gross target is genuine, and $3.3bn of that genuine part is already delivered. The rest ($0.7-1.7bn gross) arrives by end-2027, against about $0.5bn a year of inflation on the remaining cost base. The net gain to EBITDA against FY2025 is therefore about $0.4bn in 2027 and $0.8-0.9bn a year in 2028-30. Further cuts would put reliability at risk: BP achieved its 2025 upstream reliability of 96.1% with more staff than it has now.

Feedback loops: three balancing loops dominate the top of BP's income statement, and one reinforcing loop dominates the bottom.

  • Balancing, the commodity itself: high prices destroy demand, draw a supply response, invite windfall taxes, and release stranded Gulf barrels when the Strait reopens.
  • Balancing, refining capacity: high margins bring idle refineries back, bring new Asian and Middle East plants on stream and erode demand.
  • Balancing, the LNG supply wave of more than 150m tonnes a year over 2026-28.
  • Balancing, "shrink to delever": disposals remove about $2.6bn of EBITDA for about $0.5bn of interest saving.
  • Reinforcing, deleveraging into buybacks: lower debt cuts interest, which raises free cash flow, which funds buybacks, which raise EPS and dividend capacity and lower the cost of equity (figure below).

Working capital adds a one-off, counter-cyclical cushion: about $3bn is released in 2027 in the base case and about $5bn in the bear path, against a Gulf of America settlement payment of about $4.9bn that runs through BP's working-capital line.

So what: BP's revenue growth does produce outsized profit growth, but through price rather than volume, so the leverage works equally hard in reverse. From FY2026 to FY2028 revenue falls 24%, EBITDA 36%, net income 54% and EPS 53%. The reinforcing loop offsets only 10-15 points of that EPS fall, although it fully protects the dividend and the balance sheet.

Market view and mine. The market has BP's price sensitivities (every broker uses them) and describes the deleveraging loop in words. It has not modelled the floor under BP's finance cost (consensus FY2028 finance cost is $2.1bn), nor the arithmetic that makes buybacks worth two to three times debt repayment. I differ from the market in giving these mechanics more weight and in giving almost no credit to the gross cost figure. What would change my view: disclosure of trading profit and refining capture by segment from 2027, which would show whether BP's mid-chain franchise has a structural floor.

Conclusion on #5: BP has the sector's highest price leverage on a fixed cost base and no pricing power, so revenue and profit move together and are now moving down; the one lever that compounds per share, deleveraging turning into buybacks, is real, mechanical and worth about 10-15 points of EPS over the fade.

Score: 50, set by the Rater. The structure has very high operating leverage to price (about $21bn of fixed operating cost plus $17bn of depreciation against price-set revenue; $340m per $1 Brent, $450m per $1 RIM) but no pricing power at all, balancing loops at the top of the account (supply response, refinery restarts, the LNG wave) and only small net cost-out ($0.4-0.9bn a year); the one reinforcing loop, deleveraging turning into buybacks, is real and worth 10-15 points of EPS. Gearing that runs entirely on an exogenous price and is now running in reverse (revenue -24%, EPS -53% FY2026-28) is not a model where growth reliably converts into outsized profit, so the ordinary middle, coherent with the economic-strength group's 32 lifted by the financial-leverage engine; no anchors.

#6 Forecast financials; scope for double-digit growth; scope for higher growth or margins than the past

The forecasts describe a fade from a FY2026 peak to a FY2028-30 plateau. The table sets out the model's base case, on the brokers' basis of underlying profit, with the Analyst's cross-check and consensus.

The table supports three readings.

Reading 1: there is no double-digit growth in headline EPS, but there is a step-up against the pre-windfall base. EPS falls 37% in FY2027 and 26% in FY2028 before flattening. The FY2028-30 plateau of $0.62-0.67, however, is 25-40% above FY2024-25 EPS of $0.48-0.54, at a similar Brent price ($70-72 against $69-80). EPS holds flat on the plateau while net income drifts down 8%, because the share count falls about 6-8% over 2028-30. The step-up comes from the corporate changes and is mechanical. Of the $2.3bn rise in net income from FY2025 to FY2028, about $1.7bn comes from lower depreciation (assets held for sale stop depreciating, and impairments shrink the asset base), $1.4bn from lower finance cost, $0.5bn from a lower tax rate (40% falling to 37%) and $0.25bn from lower hybrid coupons, offset by $0.5bn less EBITDA. Richard should therefore read plateau EPS alongside plateau free cash flow per share, which is about $0.63-0.65, roughly equal to EPS and 1.7 times the dividend, and which is not flattered by lower depreciation.

Reading 2: margins will be no higher than in the past, but returns will be higher on a smaller capital base. The plateau EBITDA margin of 19.6% sits inside the FY2023-25 range of 19.3-20.8%. Plateau EBITDA of $35-36bn is slightly below the FY2024-25 level of $37-38bn, because businesses producing $2.6bn of EBITDA have been sold. BP will beat its target of ROACE above 16% at $70 Brent because disposals of about $15bn and impairments of about $10bn have shrunk the capital base, not because of operating outperformance.

Reading 3: our base case is close to consensus on EPS but differs in composition. Our EPS is 0.4% below consensus in FY2026, 0.7% above in FY2027, 4.6% below in FY2028 and 6.7% above in FY2029. For FY2026 the comparison predates the Q3 beat: the Analyst's $1.46 is the better figure, and consensus is moving to $1.43-1.46. FY2029 consensus rests on only ten brokers and an inconsistent share count. Our EBITDA is 4-8% below consensus in FY2027-29, and we recover the gap through tax, depreciation and share count. The composition therefore differs more than the total: we have lower operating profit, a lower tax rate, a higher FY2028 finance cost and fewer shares. At a flat $70 Brent and $12 RIM from 2027, our FY2027 EPS would be about $0.60-0.65, a third below consensus, so the model's base case describes a slow normalisation, not an immediate one.

Counter-case. The upside to these forecasts comes from the forward curve proving right (FY2027 EPS about $1.20) and from a Shell-sized buyback framework (FY2030 EPS about $0.74). The downside comes from a $65 normal Brent (FY2029 EPS about $0.49) and a calm year for trading (-$0.055 a share).

Market view and mine. The market's FY2028 median EPS of $0.67 (mean $0.65) is about right on our price assumptions and 5-10% too high at a flat $70 Brent. I agree with consensus on FY2028 on our assumptions, and I differ on FY2027 (where we sit below the forward curve) and on the share count (where we have fewer shares). What would change my view: the 2027 operating-cost outturn and the first quarter reported on the two-segment basis (May 2027), which will show whether trading and refining capture have a floor.

Conclusion on #6: the forecasts describe a peak-to-plateau fade with EPS halving by FY2028, no margin improvement on the past, and a 25-40% per-share step-up against the pre-windfall base that comes entirely from below EBIT and from the share count; there is no double-digit growth on offer, but there is a higher, better-funded floor.

Score: 18, set by the Rater. Falling gives F. I place it in the upper part of the band, not near the floor, because the fall is a windfall peak rolling off to a plateau of $0.62-0.67 that sits 25-40% above FY2024-25 at a similar deck, but that step-up is entirely below EBIT and share count, with plateau EBITDA margin of 19.6% inside the FY2023-25 range and no organic growth; coherent with the financial-forecasts group's 22.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6-12 months

Evidence: four facts point to further upgrades, and three suggest the sell-side has already caught up.

  • For upgrades: FY2026 consensus EPS of $1.37 before Q3 implied Q4 profit of only $3.9bn, against our $5.5bn and Redburn's implied $5.1bn, after actual profit of $17.4bn in the first nine months; consensus is moving to $1.43-1.46 as stale July estimates refresh.
  • For upgrades: as recently as April, several brokers modelled no buybacks at all until 2029, and a framework will add them.
  • For upgrades: our tax rate of 36-37% sits below the 40%-plus that consensus implies.
  • For upgrades: net debt at end-2026 will beat the $14-18bn target by $8-12bn.
  • Against: FY2027 consensus EPS has already risen 35% in three months, and about 10% more after Q3, the largest post-results upgrade in the sector.
  • Against: FY2027 consensus now sits at perhaps $0.92-0.95, above our $0.86.
  • Against: consensus follows a 2027 forward curve (Brent $88, refining margin $28) that sits well above our base case.

Inference. The window for upgrades is real, narrow and front-loaded. Two events can still surprise favourably. On 15 December BP should announce the buyback framework, a raised cost target, total obligations below $35bn and new 2028-30 targets set at $70-75 Brent. In February the Q4 results should show FY2026 EPS of about $1.45, net debt of $3-6bn and the first buyback tranche, with 2027 guidance set at a planning price far below the H1 2027 forward curve. From the Q1 2027 results in May, oil prices and margins take over. If the Strait reopens in stages, FY2027 consensus is cut 10-20% through the year and FY2028 consensus 5-10%, with the cuts concentrated after the Q1 and Q2 results. The first quarter reported on the two-segment basis will also have no clean comparator, which will obscure any beats.

So what: scope for upgrades exists on the per-share, balance-sheet and tax lines and over the next three months, but not on the operating lines, where our base case is already at or below where consensus is heading. The narrative upgrade still available is a shift from a "deleveraging story" to a "distribution story". Shell achieved that shift in 2023, and BP's discount to Shell on 2027 total cash yield (5.9% against 10.1%) is waiting for it.

Counter-case. If the forward curve holds, FY2027 consensus is not cut at all, our base case is too low by a third, BP reaches net cash by mid-2027, and the framework is more generous because the cash is there. Two brokers nonetheless judge the good news to be in the price already. Jefferies (19 October) judged that the sell-side had captured the near-term upside and that further upgrades need a strategic catalyst; the December framework is that catalyst. Morgan Stanley (12 October) judged that record margins were "already priced into consensus", with "little room for payout surprises".

Market view and mine. The market expects a buyback restart and a strong FY2026 close. I expect the same, and I also expect revisions to the operating lines to turn negative within six months, which the market's breadth of revisions does not yet reflect. Our view is therefore favourable relative to consensus for the next two events and unfavourable for the four after them. What would change my view: the 2027 Brent curve staying above $85 through February, in which case beats in H1 2027 would extend the favourable window by two quarters.

Conclusion on #7: scope for upgrades is real but confined to the balance-sheet, per-share and tax lines and to the next two events, after which the deck is likely to cut FY2027 consensus by 10-20% toward and then below our base.

Score: 34, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely raised only on balance-sheet and distribution lines (the 15 December framework, obligations below $35bn, possibly a raised cost target), with a measured framework about as likely to disappoint as please, while de facto operating guidance (Q4 production, throughput, a stale 2030 range) leans lower; FY2027 consensus EPS, the price-driving line, has already risen 35-40% in three months (98th percentile, now momentum not scope), sits at $0.92-0.95 above the memo's $0.86, and is likely cut 10-20% from the Q1-Q2 2027 prints, so on the memo's 30/45/25 deck probabilities the expected change is about -10% against falling revenue. One favourable burst then net negative revisions inside the window, below the fourth-set group's 44 because the cut falls on the line that drives the price, between Alfen and TT Electronics.

#8 Current momentum in guidance, sell-side, narrative, share price technicals; and the same for key peers

Evidence (dashboard, 29 October): momentum is strong on every measure, but BP is the laggard among its peers.

  • Sell-side earnings momentum, grade B: FY2027 EPS revisions +14% over one month and +35% over three; EBITDA revisions +4% and +13%; target price +2% and +7%; 54% of analysts rate BP a buy, up 10 points in three months and 20 in six; revision-momentum score 15.
  • Technical momentum, grade B: the share price of 624.3p is 17% above a 200-day average (532p) that has risen in each of the last twelve months, and within 2% of its 52-week high; relative strength is at the 82nd percentile of the universe; the 12-month return is +39.5%.
  • Guidance momentum: positive on every balance-sheet item (targets pulled forward and then beaten) and neutral on operations (Q4 production and refining throughput guided lower, and trading described as "weaker").
  • Narrative: "the clearest play on de-gearing" (Morgan Stanley), "windfall working" (Jefferies), "a simpler business and more to come" (Redburn, Neutral).
  • Peers: all five main peers (Shell, TotalEnergies, Eni, Equinor and Repsol) grade B on technical momentum, three of them grade A on sell-side momentum, and all have outperformed BP over twelve months, with returns of +40% to +95% (detail in the peer table in #12). BP's revision momentum is strong but not the sector's strongest, and its price return is the weakest among the integrated majors.
+2.4% vs +12.2%six-month return, BP against the peer basket
73%of BP's daily variance explained by the basket
1.18beta to the sector
97thpercentile of its five-year forward multiple

Inference. BP's momentum is the momentum of a rising sector tide, and BP rides it at the bottom of the fleet. The part of BP's return specific to BP has been negative, held back by leadership turnover, the suspended buyback and the priority given to the Gulf of America payable, which is consistent with a market that rewards distributions and penalises complexity. The de-rating has probably already begun. The dashboard price is dated 29 October; Brent then fell 16% in the three days to 4 November, and the two-year-forward multiple was 10.8x on 6 November against 12.1x on 25 October. Part of that fall in the multiple reflects consensus EPS rising after Q3, but part is probably a fall in the share price.

So what. Precedents show what tends to follow a peak like this one. In BP's own 2023-25, a beat in Q1 2023 was followed by six quarters of misses and downgrades as markets calmed. Across the sector in 2022-23, European majors' share prices fell 10-40% in the twelve months after the earnings peak, even as their forward multiples expanded. On our price assumptions, the breadth of revisions has one more positive burst available (December and February) and then turns negative from Q2 2027. BP's revisions will be the most volatile in the peer group in both directions, because refining and trading carry so much weight in its earnings.

Counter-case. Momentum regimes last longer than fundamentals suggest. BP's 200-day average has risen for a year, investor positioning in energy is at the 69th percentile rather than the 90th, short interest is only 0.4% of the shares, and if the forward curve is right the breadth of upgrades stays positive through mid-2027.

Market view and mine. The market reads BP's momentum as a trade in which BP catches up with its peers, with a catalyst in December. I read it as late-cycle sector momentum with a drag specific to BP that the buyback framework can turn positive, but only briefly. What would change my view: a December framework of $1bn a quarter or more, together with a 2027 Brent curve holding above $85, which would extend positive revision breadth into H2 2027.

Conclusion on #8: momentum is strong and broad today on sell-side, technical and guidance measures, but it is sector-driven, BP is the laggard in it, and on our deck it reverses on the operating lines within six months.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Both measures in the top fifth with no part negative gives A: FY2027 EPS revisions +14%/+35% over one and three months (98th percentile at three), buy share up 20 points in six months, balance-sheet guidance pulled forward and beaten, narrative improving, the price 17% above a 200-day average rising for twelve months and within 2% of its high, peers uniformly strong. Placed at the floor because BP is the laggard among its peers (six-month return +2.4% against +12.2%), operating guidance is neutral to softer, and Brent fell 16% in the three days after the dashboard date.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations

BP's case is simple to model and very hard to forecast.

Simplicity of the case and its drivers. The case is unusually simple to state and to model. Three published sensitivities explain about 90% of the variance in pre-tax profit, the changes to BP's portfolio are known, and the balance-sheet lines are guided with hard numbers and dates. The case has no second thesis in reserve, however: if oil prices and margins disappoint, the per-share mechanics cushion EPS by 10-15 points and nothing else does.

Fragilities, assumptions and requirements. About four fifths of the forecast rests on strengths BP has demonstrated: balance-sheet execution, disposals, capital discipline, and refining and trading in dislocated markets. About one fifth rests on strengths BP has not demonstrated:

  • converting gross savings into lower absolute cost;
  • earning above consensus in calm markets;
  • delivering deepwater projects on schedule in a tight supply chain (Kaskida and Tiber carry 6-12 months of slippage risk and face a lawsuit from Earthjustice);
  • sustaining a buyback through a downturn in oil prices, which BP has failed to do twice in six years.

The forecast asks little of the first three and a lot of the last, which matters most for the per-share story.

Suddenness, predictability, trackability, prevalence and materiality. The main risk is not a tail risk. A settlement that reopens the Strait of Hormuz has a medium-to-high probability over 18 months (the bear path alone carries 30%). It would re-price oil and margins in days: the 16% fall in Brent over three days to 4 November was the tenth largest in the contract's history. It would also move BP about 1.2 times as far as the sector. Oil prices and margins are perfectly trackable, but the three internal lines that could fail (trading, refining capture and net cost savings) are the least disclosed, and the move to two segments from January 2027 will obscure them further. The disclosed metrics will therefore look better over the next six months than the undisclosed ones. The figure below ranks the sudden, high-magnitude risks beyond oil prices and margins, and the two upside tails.

Sector and cyclical precedents. After the 2022 earnings peak, every major's shares fell over the following twelve months, by between 4% and 40% (chart below), while European forward P/Es expanded from about 5.4x to 6.2x because earnings fell faster than share prices. In 2014 Statoil traded at 11.4x forward earnings, against an 8.9x average, before a downgrade cycle that cut forecasts by a third. Companies that bought back shares heavily at the 2011 and 2022 peaks on levered balance sheets fared worse than those that deleveraged first. BP did so in both cycles: it bought back $10bn of shares at 20.5% gearing in 2022 and then suspended buybacks in February 2026. Shell, by contrast, cut net debt from $79bn to $45bn while distributing $26bn in 2022, and Chevron carried $10bn of net cash into 2012.

The lesson for the December framework is that a payout set as a share of cash flow on low gearing "flexes rather than breaks". BP's dividend breakeven, $60-65 Brent on 2025 arithmetic, falls to about $53-56 from 2028, once the Gulf of America payments end and interest and hybrid coupons fall.

How far to a fair trough: 30-50% below today's price. The model's FY2029 EPS of $0.62 at the ten-year median multiple of 9.5x gives about 440p (-30%). Bear-path EPS of $0.43-0.50 at 9.5x gives about 305-355p (-43% to -51%). Four outside anchors agree: the 52-week low of 413p, set with Brent in the $60s and buybacks just suspended; Jefferies' downside case of 320p; Morgan Stanley's bear case of about 327p; and a cyclical low in enterprise value to debt-adjusted cash flow (EV/DACF) near 3.8x, against 4.2-5.5x today.

Market view and mine. The market knows the risk to oil prices and margins and calls it priced ("longer disruption priced out", Morgan Stanley, 5 November), and it treats the balance-sheet floor as making BP safer than its peers. I agree about the floor. I disagree that a multiple of 10.8x, at the 64th percentile of ten years and the 97th percentile of five years, on a stock with a beta of 1.18, has priced a normalisation that halves EPS. What would change my view: a December framework with an explicit low-price guardrail that the market believes, which would turn the per-share leg of the case from an acquired strength into a demonstrated one.

Conclusion on #9: the case is simple to model and very hard to forecast: a cone of plus or minus 45-50% around FY2027-28 EPS, driven by two external prices that re-price in days, with a predictable balance-sheet floor underneath that protects the dividend and credit but not the share price.

Score: 23, set by the Rater. The case is simple to model (three published sensitivities explain about 90% of pre-tax variance; balance-sheet lines are guided with dates) but the memo's cone is plus or minus 45-50% on FY2027-28 EPS, driven by two external prices that re-price in days (Brent fell 16% in three days), with the sector's highest refining and trading gearing, a 1.18 beta to a sector near the top of its multiple range, untrackable trading and capture lines and a buyback BP has failed to hold twice in six years; the repaired balance sheet protects dividend and credit, not the share price. Coherent with the risk groups' 26 and 30: a single exogenous-input case with a range well over a third either way, at Fugro's cyclical-outlook risk and below Entra.

#10 Where the stock plausibly is in its lifecycle

Evidence. The dashboard's rule puts BP in the Broadening phase, and two of the three strands of evidence fit that label. The balance-sheet thesis fits: it turned up in 2025 (Elliott's arrival and the February reset), was confirmed through 2026 as every target was beaten early, and is now broadening into a distribution thesis that the December framework should formalise. The share price fits: twelve months of a rising 200-day average, +40% over a year, a 52-week high in late October, positive revision breadth and a rising share of buy ratings. The earnings cycle does not fit. FY2026 is the peak, every forecast fades from here, the forward multiple is at the 64th percentile of its ten-year range and the 97th of its five-year range, and the two sector digests describe the sector as caught in a "record-margin trap". The part of BP's return specific to BP has also been negative: BP has lagged the peer basket by 10 points over six months.

Inference: BP is in two lifecycle phases at once, and the sequencing of the two decides the next nine months. The corporate-change leg is late in the Broadening phase and is about to be tested by its first buyback framework. The operating-earnings leg is at the top of the Reinforcing phase and is about to Stall as oil prices and margins normalise, with sell-side revisions following from Q2 2027. For a stock whose price has a 73% R-squared with its sector, the blend is "Broadening, with a risk of stalling within six months". The question that matters is whether the distribution framework (15 December, with a first tranche in February) lands before falling oil prices and margins turn revisions negative (Q2 2027). On our price assumptions it does, by about one quarter, which is why the next three months are the favourable window and the six months after them are not.

So what: the better entry into BP is the next lifecycle phase, possibly in late 2027. In Viewforth's framework a Broadening phase earns a higher fair multiple (the guideline is the 80th percentile of the stock's own history). That multiple is right for the balance-sheet leg and generous for the earnings leg. The more attractive setup is a BP whose share price has stalled on normalised earnings, with the buyback framework running and already tested against lower oil prices and margins. That is when the "Delivering, mechanical EPS upgrader" version of BP would be on offer.

Counter-case. If the forward curve is right and the framework is generous, BP stays clearly in the Broadening phase through 2027: beats continue, the discount to Shell closes, and the shares re-rate toward 12-13x on EPS that is not falling. I put the probability of that outcome at about one in four.

Market view and mine. The market reads BP as Broadening, citing rising investor positioning, a rising share of buy ratings and a "catch-up to Shell". I agree on the balance-sheet leg, and I put the earnings leg at a peak, which the market knows but has not yet acted on. What would change my view: FY2027 consensus holding through the Q1 2027 results, which would mean the forward curve was right and the earnings stall is a question for 2028.

Conclusion on #10: Broadening on the balance-sheet and distribution leg, peaking on the earnings leg, so late-Broadening with a high probability of stalling within six months as the deck normalises; the more attractive phase for this stock is the one after the stall.

Score: 32, set by the Rater. The computed Broadening reads the balance-sheet leg and price momentum correctly but misreads the earnings leg: FY2026 is the peak, EPS falls 37% in FY2027, the good news is known to the sell-side, and revisions turn negative from Q2 2027, so the memo's 'late-Broadening with a high probability of stalling within six months' is right and the next 6-12 months bring the first large decline. The December framework keeps it off the Stalling-to-Collapsing end, placing it between D'Ieteren's Stalling and Imperial Brands' ex-growth stall.

#11 The fair multiple

The guideline and the history. Viewforth's guideline multiple for the Broadening phase is 12.82x two-year-forward EPS. That is the 80th percentile of BP's own ten-year history (10th percentile 6.0x, median 9.5x, 75th percentile 12.1x, 90th percentile 15.0x) and 19% above the 10.8x of 6 November. The history shows that BP's forward P/E moves counter-cyclically. It sat at 12-15x in 2017-18, when oil was recovering from $50 and forward earnings were depressed; it fell to 5-6x in 2022, when earnings peaked; and it climbed back to 10-13x through 2025-26, as the sector re-rated and forward EPS, which already embeds the normalisation, lagged the share price. Forward multiples on oil majors expand as earnings fade, because share prices fall less than estimates. The direction the guideline assumes, a higher multiple as EPS normalises, is therefore consistent with precedent.

My view of the level: the guideline is at the generous end of what I would pay, and I centre at 11.5-12.5x, about 12x.

Reasons to sit below the guideline

  • The starting multiple already reflects the sector's re-rating (Shell 10.0x at its 70th percentile, Eni 10.7x at its 63rd, Equinor 12.3x at its 81st), so the counter-cyclical expansion has less room than in 2017-18.
  • Plateau EPS is ex-growth: BP has the lowest reserve life among majors, and its answer on volume arrives only in 2029-30.
  • BP is a 1.18-beta proxy for a sector near the top of its range, so a reversion in the sector's multiple takes BP's multiple with it, whatever the framework says.
  • The per-share floor that would justify a premium, a buyback that holds at $60-65 Brent, is not yet demonstrated.

Reasons to sit above the median

  • The balance sheet is now in line with peers', and the dividend is covered down to about $53-56 Brent.
  • Plateau EPS is 25-40% above the pre-windfall base.
  • The activist and the board are aligned on distributions.
  • A credible framework is the one company-specific event that can narrow BP's discount to Shell and TotalEnergies by one to two multiple points.

History brackets the answer. In phases of peak delivery (2017-18, with buybacks running and a 6% dividend yield) BP's shares earned 12-15x; in stalling phases (2019 and 2023-24) they earned 7-11x. BP now sits between those, moving from the first toward the second on earnings while moving the other way on the balance sheet.

What the choice of multiple is worth: each multiple point is worth about 46-49p a share. On the model's FY2029 EPS of $0.62, 12.82x gives about $7.95, or 593p; 12.0x gives about 555p; and the median of 9.5x gives about 440p. On the Analyst's cross-check EPS of $0.66, 12.82x gives 632p and 12.0x gives 591p.

Market view and mine. The market pays 10.8x today for a two-year-forward EPS that already embeds most of the normalisation, and that is a judgement on the sector rather than on BP: the dashboard rates the valuation of BP, Shell, Eni and Repsol alike at D. I think 12x is fair for a repaired, ex-growth integrated major with a measured buyback; 12.8x needs a credible framework and a normal Brent price of $70 or better; and anything above 13x needs volume growth that BP does not have. What would change my view: a framework set at 40% or more of cash flow with a stated guardrail, which would move my central multiple up to the guideline.

Conclusion on #11: the guideline 12.82x is the upper end of fair for a late-Broadening stock whose earnings are about to stall; my central multiple is about 12x, above the ten-year median because the balance sheet and dividend floor are new, and below the guideline because the per-share leg is unproven and the sector multiple is already near its top.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C. Placed in the lower half of the band because both readings lean dear and the five-year forward multiple is at the 97th percentile, and a stock about to stall on earnings deserves a median rather than a Broadening multiple; held above the floor because the memo's own fair multiple (about 12x) is above the 10.8x of 6 November and the repaired balance sheet deserves more than BP's old history.

#12 Total shareholder return

The model's return at the guideline multiple: -1.1% to 31 December 2027 and +6.8% to 30 June 2029. The model starts from a price of 638p and a two-year-forward P/E of 12.1x on 25 October, rising to 12.82x.

  • To 31 December 2027 (18 months): -1.1% in total (-0.9% a year). Dividends add 6.2% and the rise in the multiple from 12.1x to 12.82x adds 6.3%, but earnings subtract 12.8%, because two-year-forward EPS rolls from a FY2027-28 blend of about $0.71 to FY2029's $0.62. Value per share including dividends: 632p.
  • To 30 June 2029 (three years): +6.8% in total (+2.5% a year). Dividends add 10.5% and the multiple 6.3%, while earnings subtract 9.4%, as the window rolls onto a FY2030-31 blend of about $0.64. Value per share including dividends: 682p.

The multiple and earnings components multiply, and dividends add, so the three components do not sum exactly to the total.

In plain words: there is no capital growth in the base case, and all of the return is income. Over 18 months the return is a tug of war between a 13% fall in the earnings to which the multiple is applied and a 6% rise in the multiple. The two almost cancel, leaving the 6% dividend, less a small net loss, as the return. Over three years the earnings fall is smaller, because the plateau is flat and buybacks hold EPS, so the dividends accumulate to a 7% total. The whole case for owning the shares at this price therefore rests on the multiple expanding while earnings fall, which the guideline assumes and the history permits but does not promise.

My view of the return, and its cone: close to zero on a probability-weighted basis, with a negative skew. At my central 12x and the model's EPS, the 18-month total return is about -7% (a price of 555p plus 6% of dividends) and the three-year return is about zero; at 12x on the Analyst's cross-check EPS, the returns are about -1% and +3%. The cone of outcomes is wide. The bull path (the forward curve is right and the framework is Shell-sized; FY2029 EPS about $0.80 at 12.82x) gives about 765p plus dividends, roughly +26% over 18 months. The bear path (a $65 normal Brent with a cautious framework; FY2029 EPS about $0.50 at the 9.5x median) gives about 355p plus dividends, roughly -38%. The bull path therefore pays about two thirds of what the bear path costs.

How BP's return components compare with peers'. Shell, TotalEnergies and Eni offer 2027 total cash yields of 9-10%, against BP's 5.9% (about 7.7% on our $4.5bn buyback), from frameworks already running on balance sheets already repaired. Their consensus EPS fades are also shallower: -9% to -17% in FY2027, against -37% for BP. BP's distinctive return component is the convergence of its multiple toward peers' if the framework is credible, worth 10-15% once, and that is the component with the least evidence behind it today.

Market view and mine. The consensus target price (654.6p on the dashboard; a FactSet median of 900 cents, about 672p) implies about 5-8% upside plus the dividend, close to the model's three-year return compressed into one year. I think the market's one-year number is about right in level and wrong in shape: the return is more likely to be negative over the first 12 months, as oil prices and margins normalise and the framework is tested, and positive after that. What would change my view: a December framework strong enough to lift my fair multiple to the guideline, which would make the 18-month return about +5% on the Analyst's cross-check EPS and would change the shape from "down, then up" to "flat, then up".

Conclusion on #12: at the guideline multiple the shares return about -1% over 18 months and +7% over three years, all of it dividend, because the two-year-forward earnings fall 13% while the multiple is assumed to rise 6%; on my 12x the 18-month return is about -7%, and the probability-weighted return is near zero with a negative skew.

Score: 21, set by the Rater. A small loss gives F, about 21 on the scale for -5%; the three-year check (+7% at the guideline, about nil at the memo's 12x) and a return made entirely of the 6% dividend confirm there is no capital growth in the base case. Held near the top of the band rather than lower because the loss is small and the bull path is real, but the lower tail is fat and fast (the bear path costs half as much again as the bull pays).

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

BP today is a well-run repair of a mid-ranked business, financed by a windfall that is about to end.

The repair is real, early and almost complete. The balance sheet that made BP the sector's most fragile major for a decade is now in line with peers', the dividend is safe down to Brent in the mid-$50s, and the per-share arithmetic of interest, hybrid coupons, tax, depreciation and buybacks lifts normalised EPS by a quarter to two fifths above the pre-windfall base.

The windfall is also real, and it is about to normalise. Refining and trading, 28% of FY2026 EBITDA against a 9% norm, will revert within weeks once the Strait reopens, Brent will follow, and EPS will halve to a plateau of about $0.62-0.67 by FY2028.

The share price follows the windfall, not the repair, because BP is a 1.18-beta proxy for a sector priced near the top of its range. The sell-side already knows both halves of the case, and its remaining errors (the finance-cost floor, the tax rate, the depreciation uplift, and the arithmetic of buybacks against debt repayment) are small and roughly offset each other. The next two events are favourable and the four after them are not. At the guideline multiple the shares offer their dividend and nothing else over 18 months, and at my fair multiple a little less than that. The cone around that outcome is plus or minus 45-50% on EPS, skewed down in both speed and consequence.

For Richard, three conclusions follow.

  1. BP is not a positively skewed upgrade case over 12-24 months. The probabilities are balanced, but the downside arrives faster, and the known catalyst in December is as likely to disappoint the bulls as to please them.
  2. The version of BP worth owning is forming. It is an ex-growth integrated major with a repaired balance sheet and a running buyback, priced on normalised earnings after oil prices and margins have reset: a "Delivering, mechanical EPS upgrader" setup that could be on offer in late 2027, at a lower share price and a lower multiple.
  3. The one development that would bring that timetable forward is the forward curve proving right about 2027 refining margins. That is a one-in-four event that would reveal itself quarter by quarter, and Richard should watch for it in the January trading statement and through the Q2 2027 refinery maintenance season.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 36, set by the Rater. The internal reset (topic 2, 70) is strong, funded and reaches per-share profit through interest, hybrids, tax, depreciation and buybacks, but the external windfall reversing (topic 1, 27) is larger in magnitude and halves EPS to FY2028, so the financial outputs (topic 6, F, 18) are falling rather than sufficiently improving; net change is negative, cushioned because the plateau sits 25-40% above the pre-windfall base, which is why I sit well below the Analyst's B.

Foundations' Robustness: 37, set by the Rater. A mid-ranked price-taker with cyclical mid-chain advantages, the lowest reserve life among majors and below-peer normal returns (topic 3, 35) is a mediocre business now made safe by a repaired balance sheet and a dividend covered to the mid-$50s, and its delivery record (topic 4, 47) is excellent on balance-sheet lines but includes six to eight quarters of misses and a suspended buyback inside three years; robust to survive, not robust in earnings, so below the Analyst's C.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 40, set by the Rater. The case fits a Big Corporate Change-driven EPS Upgrader in kind (new external CEO, activist, $20bn disposals, deleveraging, a buyback framework due) but misses the setup's central element, rising EPS: the step-up is below-EBIT and mechanical and is overwhelmed by a headline EPS that halves as the windfall reverses, and today's operating problems (reliability, process safety, cost leakage) blur the change; a loose fit between the 25 and 50 levels, a little below the Analyst's C.

Case Riskiness: 24, set by the Rater. Over topic 9 (23): a simple, trackable but single-driver case whose EPS cone is plus or minus 45-50% on two external prices that move in days, at a 1.18 beta to a sector near the top of its range; the balance sheet now prevents a miss becoming a credit or dividend problem, which holds it above the 10 level, consistent with the Analyst's D.

End notes

Prices, currency and dates. The share price used throughout is 624.3p on 29 October 2026, from the dashboard (52-week high 638.5p). The model's own price is 638p on 25 October, which it converts to $8.55, so this memo uses an exchange rate of $1.34 to the pound throughout. All money is in US dollars unless stated.

Definitions. "Underlying" profit is BP's underlying replacement-cost profit attributable to shareholders, the basis the brokers use. "RIM" is BP's refining indicator margin. "The deck" means the assumed path of oil prices, refining margins and trading conditions. "Perimeter" changes are the effects of disposals and acquisitions. "The model" is the Financial Analyst's model after update 2, whose forecasts this memo uses; "our base case" is the same model's base case.

The two EPS series. Where the Analyst's own EPS cross-check differs from the model (FY2026 EPS of $1.46 against $1.36; FY2029-30 EPS of $0.66-0.67 against $0.62-0.63), the memo quotes both. The gaps are mechanical, not differences of view: the cross-check uses the tax actually reported in each quarter of FY2026, and it assumes buybacks retire shares at a lower price than the model does.

Probabilities and tables. The bear, base and bull probabilities (30%, 45% and 25%) are those set in the third round of the analysis. Richard's five standard financial tables (annual history, recent periods, FactSet consensus, broker detail and segments) are placed beside the text each one best supports.

Note on the forecast inputs. I changed none of the model's inputs. I considered three. First, the FY2027 refining path (our RIM of $17, against a forward curve near $28 and Morgan Stanley's $27.7): I kept it, because the memo's argument about skew needs the base case to sit below the curve on the most reversible line, and the gap is set out in #1, #6 and the first judgement. Second, the FY2027 buyback: the third and fourth rounds of the analysis already lowered it to $4.5bn, which matches my reading of the December framework in #4. Third, the tax rate of 36-37%: it is below consensus, and BP's Q3 tax rate of 28% and its 31-34% guidance support it. The model's two mechanical gaps to the Analyst's cross-check (FY2026 tax on reported quarters, and the price at which buybacks retire shares) are matters for the Financial Analyst, not input changes, and I have quoted both EPS series where the difference matters. No `inputs-changed.md` is written.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
